description:
Wesam Saad examines objections to unconditional election through the biblical passages used in this series. After reviewing total depravity, he explains that unconditional election does not mean salvation without faith. His claim concerns the basis of God’s choice: God does not choose because of a person’s qualities or a foreseen independent decision. He distinguishes foreknowledge as a relationship from merely knowing future information and tests that reading against Peter’s description of Christ as foreknown. Passages about Christ knowing his people and the Father giving people to the Son develop the argument. Saad asks listeners to explain the textual basis rather than simply repeat a theological label.

The discussion then considers whether election concerns individuals or only nations, and whether choosing some makes God unjust. Acts 13 and the instruction to correct opponents gently are used to discuss faith and repentance as God’s gifts to particular people. Saad distinguishes mercy towards the undeserving from punishment that is justly deserved. The fuller treatment of Romans 9 is reserved for the next meeting, so this session does not complete every objection it raises. Throughout, the study calls for careful attention to Scripture and an appreciation of divine grace. Difficult questions are invited as part of learning to understand and defend the position being taught.

questions.question: Does unconditional election mean that faith is unnecessary?
questions.answer: No. Saad explicitly says a person must believe in Christ. By unconditional, he means that God’s choice is not based on personal qualities, background or an independently foreseen act of faith. In his account, God’s sovereign choice leads the person to believe rather than bypassing belief.

questions.question: How does this session connect with the preceding discussion of total depravity?
questions.answer: Saad recalls sin affecting mind, affections and will, while denying that every unbeliever is as wicked as possible. He uses this to frame the question of how the spiritually unable sinner comes to faith. Sovereign election is presented as God’s gracious initiative, not a reward for an untouched faculty within the person.

questions.question: What distinction does he make between foreknowledge and foreseeing?
questions.answer: Saad understands foreknowledge in these salvation passages relationally, rather than simply as possession of information about a future choice. He appeals to Christ’s knowledge of his own and the contrasting statement that he never knew some people. The answer describes his contextual interpretation without making a universal definition for every use of knowing.

questions.question: Why does he compare the two foreknowledge references in 1 Peter 1?
questions.answer: Saad compares election according to God’s foreknowledge with Christ being foreknown before the foundation of the world. He argues that the second reference cannot mean God discovered Christ’s future action and then selected him. This comparison challenges the foreseen-faith explanation within his reading of the chapter.

questions.question: How does he use the Father’s giving in John 6?
questions.answer: Saad follows the sequence in which the Father gives people to the Son, they come to Christ, and Christ receives and ultimately raises them. He treats coming as believing and argues that the Father’s action is prior in the explanation. The assurance is connected to those given, rather than a claim that every person will finally be saved.

questions.question: How does he answer the claim that election concerns groups rather than individuals?
questions.answer: Saad argues that groups are composed of individuals and appeals to the people appointed to eternal life who believe in Acts 13. He also uses the granting of repentance in the instruction about correcting opponents. His aim is to establish an individual dimension, while the fuller Romans 9 discussion remains ahead.

questions.question: How are the command to repent and the gift of repentance distinguished?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes the command addressed to all from God granting repentance to particular people. The passage about gentle correction also gives a practical posture for speaking with opponents: teach patiently rather than quarrel. He does not tell listeners to decide in advance who has been chosen before offering the gospel.

questions.question: How does he distinguish mercy, justice and injustice?
questions.answer: Saad argues that sinners do not possess a claim to salvation as a deserved reward. In his explanation, those saved receive mercy and those judged receive justice, so choosing some does not itself establish injustice. This is the position he defends; he reserves a closer reading of Romans 9 for the next meeting.

questions.question: How does he want listeners to handle difficult objections?
questions.answer: Saad invites questions that remain unsettled and urges listeners to explain their convictions from Scripture. His aim is understanding that can be defended and applied, accompanied by appreciation of God’s grace. The session models examining objections rather than treating knowledge of a theological acronym as sufficient.
